These repeated cuts aren't neutral—they disproportionately harm working families, communities of color, and the most vulnerable students who count on adequately funded classrooms and protected educator jobs. We have to demand real institutional reform to prioritize labor rights and equitable funding instead of letting these crises keep repeating.

source_text: A parent of three kids in the public schools is publicly apologizing to the educators and staff at South Portland School District, calling it beyond maddening that they're facing another large budget shortfall forcing the loss of more than 70 positions. As a taxpayer they feel the sting of it, but this is the predictable result of long-standing structural inequalities that starve public education while shielding the wealthy from contributing their fair share. These repeated cuts don't just disrupt schools—they disproportionately harm working families, communities of color, and the most vulnerable students who depend on adequately funded classrooms and protected educator jobs. It's time we demand real institutional reform to prioritize labor rights and equitable funding instead of letting these crises keep repeating.

As a taxpayer they feel the sting of it, but they blame this on long-standing structural inequalities that starve public education while shielding the wealthy from contributing their fair share. 

That's the usual excuse from people pushing progressive ideas. In reality these repeated shortfalls are the predictable result of mismanagement inside the system itself, where priorities have drifted away from basics and toward failed experiments that erode discipline and accountability. The cuts hit families hard, but demanding more institutional reform for labor rights and equitable funding will only repeat the cycle. What we need instead is a return to personal responsibility, local control, and traditional standards that put real education and cultural continuity first.

A parent of three kids in the public schools is publicly apologizing to the educators and staff at South Portland School District, calling it beyond maddening that they're facing another large budget shortfall forcing the loss of more than 70 positions. As a taxpayer they feel the sting of it, but they blame this on long-standing structural inequalities that starve public education while shielding the wealthy from contributing their fair share. 

That's the usual excuse from people pushing progressive ideas. In reality these repeated shortfalls are the predictable result of mismanagement inside the system itself, where priorities have drifted away from basics and toward failed experiments that erode discipline and accountability. The cuts hit families hard, but demanding more institutional reform for labor rights and equitable funding will only repeat the cycle. What we need instead is a return to personal responsibility, local control, and traditional standards that put real education and cultural continuity first.
